title: One-off events & effects
scopeHtml: Scope: the one-off event debate (Channel/SharedFlow vs events-as-state), lost and duplicated events, navigation and snackbar events, consumption, testing, and migration from SingleLiveEvent. Flow/Channel operator mechanics belong to A1; UiState modeling belongs to A4 chunk 02.

questions.promptHtml: What is a "one-off event" in an Android screen, and why did SingleLiveEvent exist?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that you understand the state-vs-event distinction that every later architecture decision hangs on.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: State is something the screen is (a list, a spinner); it can be re-rendered any number of times safely. A one-off event is something that should happen once: show a snackbar, navigate, open a dialog. LiveData is a state holder that re-delivers its last value to every new observer, so after rotation a "navigate" value fired again. SingleLiveEvent was a LiveData wrapper with an AtomicBoolean that delivered each value once. It was a workaround for using a state tool to carry events.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• LiveData and StateFlow are sticky: a new collector immediately gets the current value. That is exactly right for state, exactly wrong for "navigate to Details".
  • After a configuration change the Activity is recreated, the new observer attaches to the surviving ViewModel, and the sticky value is delivered again. Symptom: the snackbar reappears on every rotation, or the app navigates twice.
  • SingleLiveEvent (from the old architecture-samples repo) set a pending flag on setValue and cleared it on first delivery. Its known flaws: only one observer is guaranteed to get the event (others race), and if no observer is active the event waits and fires at an unpredictable later time.
State:   [Loading] -> [Success(list)] -> rotate -> observer re-attaches -> Success(list) again   (fine, idempotent)
Event:   [NavigateToDetails] -> rotate -> observer re-attaches -> NavigateToDetails again        (bug)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Classic broken usage: LiveData used as an event channel
class LoginViewModel : ViewModel() {
    private val _navigate = MutableLiveData<Boolean>()
    val navigate: LiveData<Boolean> = _navigate
    fun onLoggedIn() { _navigate.value = true }   // re-delivered after rotation
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "events are lost on rotation" as the only problem. The LiveData problem is duplication; the Flow problem is loss. Know which tool fails which way.
  • Treating SingleLiveEvent as fine because it "works" with one observer.
  • Calling every UI update an event. Most of what people call events is state.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is StateFlow not a replacement for SingleLiveEvent? -> It is sticky and conflates equal values; setting the same value twice emits once.
  2. What breaks with two observers on SingleLiveEvent? -> Whoever consumes first clears the flag; the other never sees it.
  3. Is there a delivery guarantee for any event mechanism? -> Not exactly-once across process death and not across a producer that outlives its consumer; that is why the official guidance reduces events to state.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "SingleLiveEvent fires once". The senior answer names sticky delivery as the root cause, lists its multi-observer and no-observer flaws, and frames the whole debate as "what delivery guarantee does this action need".

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A checkout screen that re-navigated to "Order placed" on every rotation produced duplicate order-confirmation analytics events and confused support tickets.

questions.promptHtml: What does Google's official architecture guidance say about ViewModel events, and how do you apply it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know the documented position, can state it accurately, and can argue with it intelligently.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The UI-events guide says UI actions that originate in the ViewModel should always result in a UI state update, so they survive configuration changes and are not lost. Events that originate in the UI and need only UI behavior (navigation click, expand a card) are handled in the UI. Events needing business logic go to the ViewModel through a function call. The guide explicitly warns that Channels and other reactive streams do not guarantee delivery when the producer outlives the consumer.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The guide's decision tree has three branches:

Where the event originates Needs Handle it
ViewModel anything Update UI state; UI reacts
UI business logic Call a ViewModel function
UI UI behavior logic only Change UI element state in the UI

Two ideas carry the guide:

  1. Separate business logic (what to do, in ViewModel/domain/data) from UI behavior logic (how to show it: navigation, snackbars; may differ on tablet vs phone).
  2. "Don't think about what actions the UI needs to take; think about how those actions affect UI state."

The guide also says that if you have multiple consumers and fear consuming an event more than once, reconsider your architecture, because exactly-once with concurrent consumers is very hard. And when state must not be consumed in the background (a Toast), consume it only when the UI is in the foreground.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
data class LoginUiState(
    val isLoginInProgress: Boolean = false,
    val errorMessage: String? = null,
    val isUserLoggedIn: Boolean = false,
)
// ViewModel sets isUserLoggedIn = true; the UI observes it and calls onSuccessfulLogin().

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Claiming the guide forbids all Channels. It says delivery is not guaranteed when the ViewModel outlives the UI; the practical reading is "do not use them where a missed event is user-visible damage".
  • Forgetting that the guide's state-based navigation example needs extra UI-held state when the source screen stays on the back stack.
  • Quoting the guide without noting it is explicitly "guidelines, adapt as needed".

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does navigation logic live? -> UI layer; the ViewModel exposes state, the caller composable receives an onNavigate lambda.
  2. What if the screen stays on the back stack after navigating forward? -> Keep a UI-level flag (e.g. rememberSaveable) so returning does not auto-advance again.
  3. Do you agree with the guide fully? -> Mostly; I would still defend a rendezvous-style effect channel for purely cosmetic effects, and say so openly (see Q060).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use StateFlow, not SharedFlow". Senior: states the decision tree, the business-vs-UI-logic split, and the multi-consumer caveat, then notes where the guidance gets awkward in practice.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that adopted the "event becomes state plus ack" rule removed an entire class of "toast after rotation" bugs but had to add ack calls in every screen; a shared helper (Q059) reduced that cost.

questions.promptHtml: Why is MutableSharedFlow<Event>() with default settings a bad channel for one-off events, and what do replay and extraBufferCapacity change?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: SharedFlow is the most common "modern SingleLiveEvent". Interviewers want to see that you know its loss and duplication modes precisely.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A MutableSharedFlow() with replay = 0 and no buffer drops (or suspends on) an emission when there are no subscribers. During rotation or while the screen is stopped there are zero collectors, so the event vanishes. Setting replay = 1 fixes the loss but brings back the duplicate: a new collector gets the replayed event again. So SharedFlow trades one failure for the other.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• MutableSharedFlow(replay, extraBufferCapacity, onBufferOverflow); defaults are 0, 0, SUSPEND.
  • With no subscribers, emit returns immediately and the value is discarded (there is nobody to wait for). tryEmit returns true in that case.
  • With subscribers and zero buffer, emit suspends until all current subscribers receive it. A slow subscriber suspends the producer.
  • replay = 1 stores the last value; every new subscriber receives it. After rotation, the new collector replays the old "ShowSnackbar" event.
  • Workarounds (replay plus a consumed flag, resetReplayCache()) re-create SingleLiveEvent's flaws with more code.
  • Multiple collectors each get every event (broadcast), which is the opposite of "exactly one consumer handles it".
replay=0:  emit -> no collector (rotating) -> dropped
replay=1:  emit -> stored -> rotate -> new collector -> same event delivered again

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class VM : ViewModel() {
    // Loses events during rotation / stopped lifecycle
    private val _events = MutableSharedFlow<UiEvent>()
    val events = _events.asSharedFlow()

    fun onPay() = viewModelScope.launch { _events.emit(UiEvent.ShowSnackbar("Paid")) }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing extraBufferCapacity helps: it buffers for existing subscribers only; with zero subscribers the value is still not retained.
  • Using replay = 1 plus distinctUntilChanged(); this suppresses legitimate repeated identical events.
  • Emitting from viewModelScope assuming the UI is listening.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does emit not suspend forever when nobody collects? -> It only waits for current subscribers; none means nothing to wait for.
  2. Can you make SharedFlow queue for a late subscriber? -> Not without replay; use a Channel if you need a queue.
  3. What breaks with repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) collection? -> Collection is cancelled below STARTED, so events emitted in that window are dropped (replay=0) or replayed later (replay>0).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "SharedFlow with replay 0 for events". Senior: shows the zero-subscriber loss window, the replay duplicate window, and explains why neither is exactly-once.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team saw "payment failed" snackbars missing for users who locked the screen mid-request; the SharedFlow emission fell in the zero-subscriber gap.

questions.promptHtml: How does a Channel consumed with receiveAsFlow() behave as an event pipe, and where does it still lose or mis-deliver events?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many codebases use Channel(BUFFERED) plus receiveAsFlow() as "the" answer. A senior should know its real guarantees.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A Channel buffers elements until a receiver takes them, so events sent while the UI is gone are queued rather than dropped, and each element goes to exactly one receiver (fan-out, not broadcast). That solves loss across rotation in the common case. It still fails when a receive is cancelled just as the element is delivered, when the process dies, and when two collectors compete.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Channel<T>(Channel.BUFFERED) has a default buffer of 64 (verify against your coroutines version) ; UNLIMITED never suspends; CONFLATED keeps only the latest; RENDEZVOUS (0) suspends send until a receiver is ready.
  • receiveAsFlow() is fan-out: with several collectors, each element goes to only one. consumeAsFlow() allows a single collection ever and cancels the channel on completion, so a second collection (after rotation) crashes or sees a closed channel.
  • Lifecycle-aware collection (repeatOnLifecycle) cancels the collector at STOPPED. A suspended receive that is cancelled has a "prompt cancellation guarantee": if the coroutine is cancelled while the element is in flight, the element can be lost. onUndeliveredElement exists on the Channel constructor to observe this.
  • Buffered events live in memory in the ViewModel; process death clears them.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class VM : ViewModel() {
    private val _effects = Channel<Effect>(Channel.BUFFERED)
    val effects = _effects.receiveAsFlow()   // not consumeAsFlow()

    fun onPay() { _effects.trySend(Effect.ShowSnackbar("Paid")) }
}

@Composable
fun Screen(vm: VM, onSnack: suspend (String) -> Unit) {
    val lifecycle = LocalLifecycleOwner.current.lifecycle
    LaunchedEffect(vm, lifecycle) {
        lifecycle.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
            vm.effects.collect { if (it is Effect.ShowSnackbar) onSnack(it.msg) }
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• consumeAsFlow() in a ViewModel: the second screen instance cannot collect.
  • Handling the effect inside a collect that suspends for a long time (a snackbar); later events wait behind it, which is fine for a queue but surprising if you expected "latest wins".
  • Assuming "buffered" means "durable".

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not trySend to an UNLIMITED channel? -> Never fails to enqueue, but unbounded memory if the UI never returns.
  2. Two collectors on one channel? -> Elements alternate between them; only one handles each event, which is almost never what you want.
  3. How would you detect lost events in production? -> onUndeliveredElement logging plus a counter metric (see Q057).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Channel is the right one". Senior: states fan-out semantics, cancellation edge, and process-death limit, and picks it only for cosmetic effects.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A screen that collected the effect Channel in two places (a composable and a helper) showed every second snackbar; the elements were being split between collectors.

questions.promptHtml: Explain the "events as state with acknowledgement" pattern. What does the ViewModel expose, and what does the UI do?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the officially recommended pattern; the signal is whether you can implement it correctly, not just name it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The ViewModel stores the pending thing in UiState, such as userMessage: String? or navigateTo: Route?. The UI renders it (shows the snackbar, navigates), then calls a ViewModel function like userMessageShown() that sets the field back to null. State survives rotation, so the UI re-reads it until acknowledged, which gives at-least-once delivery, and the ack makes it effectively once.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Producer: uiState = uiState.copy(userMessage = "No internet").
  • Consumer: LaunchedEffect(userMessage) { snackbarHostState.showSnackbar(msg); vm.userMessageShown() }.
  • Delivery is at-least-once: if the Activity is destroyed after render but before the ack, the message shows again after recreation. For snackbars that is acceptable; for "charge card" it is not, so never put side-effecting commands in UI-acked state.
  • The guide's note: consumption of a message (dismissal or timeout) is treated as user input to the ViewModel, so state remains a faithful picture of what is on screen.
  • Multiple messages: use a list with ids (the Jetsnack SnackbarManager approach) so two messages in quick succession do not overwrite each other.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
data class NewsUiState(val news: List<News> = emptyList(), val userMessage: String? = null)

class NewsViewModel : ViewModel() {
    private val _ui = MutableStateFlow(NewsUiState())
    val ui = _ui.asStateFlow()
    fun refresh() { viewModelScope.launch { _ui.update { it.copy(userMessage = "No internet") } } }
    fun userMessageShown() { _ui.update { it.copy(userMessage = null) } }
}

@Composable
fun NewsScreen(vm: NewsViewModel, snackbar: SnackbarHostState) {
    val ui by vm.ui.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    ui.userMessage?.let { msg ->
        LaunchedEffect(msg) { snackbar.showSnackbar(msg); vm.userMessageShown() }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting the ack; the message re-shows on every recomposition or rotation.
  • LaunchedEffect(Unit): a new message with the same screen instance would not retrigger.
  • Two identical consecutive messages: state equals previous state so nothing changes. Use an id or counter.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can the ack race? -> The new message may arrive between show and ack; ack by id, not by blindly nulling.
  2. What if the user dismisses after rotation? -> showSnackbar is cancelled with the composition; the message is still in state and shows again (acceptable).
  3. Does this survive process death? -> Only if the field is saved via SavedStateHandle; usually transient messages are not worth saving.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "put it in state and null it". Senior: names at-least-once, id-based ack, repeated-identical-message problem, and where this pattern is wrong (non-idempotent commands).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team nulling the message without checking the id dropped a second error that arrived while the first snackbar was animating out.

questions.promptHtml: How should a ViewModel trigger navigation, and what extra logic is needed when the source screen stays on the back stack?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Navigation is the highest-stakes "event". Double navigation and lost navigation are classic production bugs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The ViewModel does not navigate; it exposes state such as isUserLoggedIn and the UI (the caller composable that owns the NavController) reacts by invoking an onNavigate lambda. If the source screen is kept on the back stack, simply reacting to isDobValid == true would re-navigate every time the user presses Back, so UI-level state (rememberSaveable flag) records "the user asked to continue" and is cleared once navigation happens.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• UI-originated navigation (button tap): call the lambda directly. The docs recommend wrapping in dropUnlessResumed { } (lifecycle-runtime-compose; verify minimum version, 2.8.x) so rapid double taps or taps during a transition do not navigate twice.
  • ViewModel-originated (validation result): state flows to UI. React with LaunchedEffect plus snapshotFlow/flowWithLifecycle filtered on the flag, and call a rememberUpdatedState copy of the lambda so a recomposition with a new lambda does not restart the effect.
  • Why the extra flag: state isDobValid = true persists in the ViewModel. User goes A -> B -> Back to A: ViewModel still says valid, effect fires, you are pushed to B again.
  • Other fixes: ViewModel clears the flag after navigation is observed (ack, Q053), or make the validation result part of per-attempt state.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun DobScreen(onNext: () -> Unit, vm: DobViewModel = viewModel()) {
    var continuing by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf(false) }
    val currentOnNext by rememberUpdatedState(onNext)
    val ui by vm.ui.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    LaunchedEffect(ui.isDobValid, continuing) {
        if (ui.isDobValid && continuing) { continuing = false; currentOnNext() }
    }
    Button(onClick = { continuing = true; vm.validate() }) { Text("Continue") }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Passing NavController into the ViewModel (leaks the UI, untestable).
  • Navigating inside composition rather than inside an effect/callback.
  • Auto-navigating on state that is never reset.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why dropUnlessResumed? -> Taps during exit transitions can enqueue duplicate navigations; resumed-gating drops them.
  2. Why rememberUpdatedState? -> Keeps the long-lived effect calling the latest lambda without restarting.
  3. Tablet two-pane layout? -> Navigation is UI behavior logic; the same state may mean "advance" on phone and "update pane" on tablet.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "emit a navigate event". Senior: says navigation is UI logic, expresses the trigger as state, and handles the back-stack re-trigger.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A signup flow bounced users forward again each time they pressed Back, because the ViewModel's isValid stayed true.

questions.contextHtml:
A sign-in screen (480k DAU, 2% of sessions hit the bug, concentrated on slow devices and rotation-heavy tablets) uses this code. Crashlytics shows IllegalArgumentException: Navigation action/destination ... cannot be found from the current destination plus support tickets: "after login I land on Home, press Back and I am on Home again" (a double-stacked Home).

class SignInViewModel : ViewModel() {
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow(SignInState())
    val state = _state.asStateFlow()
    fun signIn(u: String, p: String) = viewModelScope.launch {
        val ok = auth.login(u, p)
        _state.value = SignInState(loggedIn = ok)
    }
}

@Composable
fun SignInScreen(nav: NavController, vm: SignInViewModel = hiltViewModel()) {
    val s by vm.state.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    if (s.loggedIn) {
        nav.navigate("home")          // runs on every recomposition
    }
    Button(onClick = { vm.signIn("a", "b") }) { Text("Sign in") }
}
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug(s), explain the production symptoms, and fix them.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use a SharedFlow instead of StateFlow." That changes the mechanism but misses that navigation is called as a side effect of composition.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is SignIn removed from the back stack on success (popUpTo)? Which API level / device mix? Any launchSingleTop? What does the crash stack show for the destination?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship a hotfix with launchSingleTop = true and popUpTo("signin") { inclusive = true } on the navigate call to stop the duplicate Home.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) nav.navigate executed in composition; any recomposition while loggedIn == true calls it again. (b) State stays loggedIn = true after navigation, so rotation or Back re-triggers it. (c) Double tap runs signIn twice. (d) Red herring: Hilt hiltViewModel() is fine here.
  4. How I'd verify each: Add a log/counter in the if; use Layout Inspector's recomposition counts; reproduce with rotation during the loading call; read Navigation back-stack via nav.currentBackStack in a debug build.
  5. Root cause: Side effects in composition run per recomposition, and composition may run many times and out of order. The "navigate" is also derived from persisting state with no ack, so it is replayed on every re-entry.
  6. Fix:
@Composable
fun SignInScreen(onSignedIn: () -> Unit, vm: SignInViewModel = hiltViewModel()) {
    val s by vm.state.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    val currentOnSignedIn by rememberUpdatedState(onSignedIn)
    LaunchedEffect(s.loggedIn) { if (s.loggedIn) currentOnSignedIn() }
    Button(onClick = dropUnlessResumed { vm.signIn("a", "b") }) { Text("Sign in") }
}
// caller: onSignedIn = { nav.navigate("home") { popUpTo("signin") { inclusive = true } } }

Long term: add an isSigningIn guard in the ViewModel so signIn is idempotent while in flight. 7. Prevention: Lint rule/code review check: no NavController calls or ViewModel mutations directly in composition; screens take onNavigate lambdas; a Compose UI test that rotates and asserts a single back-stack entry. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not add a boolean "navigated" in the ViewModel as a patch (UI concern stored in the wrong layer); here popUpTo plus an effect is enough because Sign-in leaves the back stack.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if Sign-in stays on the back stack (re-auth modal)? -> Add UI-level rememberSaveable "attempt in progress" flag like the official DOB example, or have the ViewModel ack the flag.
  • Why not LaunchedEffect(Unit)? -> It never re-runs for a later login in the same composition.
  • Would a Channel fix it? -> It would fix duplication but introduce loss in background; the effect approach is simpler.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A login screen navigated in composition and worked in debug; in release on a fast device recomposition was rarer, so the bug hid until a low-end device mix hit it. The fix was three lines; finding it took two days because the crash was in Navigation, not in the screen.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Swaps StateFlow for SharedFlow without explaining recomposition.
  • Hire: Moves navigate into an effect/lambda, adds popUpTo.
  • Strong hire: Adds idempotent signIn, explains the at-least-once nature of state-driven navigation, and proposes a lint/UI test to prevent regression.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between a "UI effect" in your architecture and a Compose "side effect"? Which APIs do you use to run one-off work in a composable safely?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The word "effect" is overloaded. Interviewers check you can separate the architectural concept from Compose mechanics.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A UI effect (MVI term) is a one-shot instruction from the presentation logic to the view: show snackbar, navigate. A Compose side effect is any change that escapes the composable's scope (a call to a navigator, a network call, registering a listener). Composition can run many times, in any order, or be discarded, so side effects must live in effect APIs: LaunchedEffect, DisposableEffect, SideEffect, rememberCoroutineScope, rememberUpdatedState. UI effects are delivered to the view; Compose effect APIs are how the view executes them.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
API Use for
LaunchedEffect(key) suspend work tied to composition; restarts when key changes, cancelled on leave
rememberCoroutineScope launching from callbacks (click handlers)
rememberUpdatedState long-lived effect that should call the latest lambda
DisposableEffect register/unregister listeners
SideEffect publish Compose state to non-Compose objects after every successful recomposition
  • Choosing the key is the design decision: LaunchedEffect(Unit) runs once per composition entry; LaunchedEffect(message) re-runs per new message.
  • Compose mechanics (recomposition, skipping) are A3's territory; here the point is where one-off work belongs.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun Screen(vm: VM, snackbar: SnackbarHostState, onDone: () -> Unit) {
    val currentOnDone by rememberUpdatedState(onDone)
    LaunchedEffect(vm) {                       // vm stable, effect lives as long as screen
        vm.effects.collect {
            when (it) {
                is Effect.Snack -> snackbar.showSnackbar(it.text)
                Effect.Done -> currentOnDone()
            }
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling snackbar.showSnackbar directly in composition (it is suspend; it will not compile) or via GlobalScope.
  • LaunchedEffect(onDone) where onDone is a new lambda each recomposition: effect restarts, may drop in-flight events.
  • Collecting effects with collectAsState; effects are not state.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why rememberCoroutineScope for clicks? -> A click handler is not in composition; you need a scope that is cancelled when the composable leaves.
  2. Does LaunchedEffect survive rotation? -> No; the composition is recreated, the effect restarts. ViewModel state is what survives.
  3. Why not do effect work in the ViewModel? -> UI-only objects (SnackbarHostState, NavController) must not live there.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: lists the APIs. Senior: explains keys as lifecycle decisions and why the architectural and Compose meanings of "effect" must not be conflated.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An effect keyed on a lambda restarted every recomposition during a list scroll and replayed the same collected event twice.

questions.promptHtml: Can you build exactly-once delivery of a ViewModel event to the UI? Walk through the failure windows for Channel, SharedFlow and state-with-ack.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: L3 candidates reason in delivery semantics rather than preferences.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Not exactly-once, because producer and consumer have independent lifetimes and the UI can die between "received" and "handled". The realistic choices are at-most-once (SharedFlow replay 0, conflated Channel) or at-least-once (state with ack). Make handlers idempotent or choose the guarantee per event: cosmetic events can be at-most-once, anything with consequences should be modeled as state.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Failure windows:

Mechanism Loss window Duplicate window
SharedFlow replay=0 no collector (rotation, STOPPED) none
SharedFlow replay=1 none until overwritten new collector replays
Channel + receiveAsFlow cancel racing delivery; process death; buffer overflow (non-UNLIMITED) none
State + ack process death (unless saved) UI destroyed after render, before ack
  • Channel's onUndeliveredElement callback is invoked when an element was sent but not received (channel cancelled or a receive cancelled mid-delivery), letting you log/measure loss.
  • Exactly-once needs a durable id: persist the pending command (Room/outbox) and make the handler idempotent by id. That is a data-layer pattern, not a UI one.
  • Rule of thumb: ask "if this is delivered zero times, is it harmful? If twice?" Snackbar: zero is mildly bad, twice is mildly bad. Navigate-after-payment: zero is dangerous (user retries payment), twice is harmful (two screens).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val effects = Channel<Effect>(
    capacity = Channel.BUFFERED,
    onUndeliveredElement = { e -> logger.warn("undelivered effect $e") },
)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using the same mechanism for toast and "payment succeeded".
  • Believing Channel.RENDEZVOUS makes the UI handle the event; it only guarantees a receiver took it.
  • Logging nothing: lost events are invisible in production.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you make payment confirmation exactly-once? -> Persist the order id/result; UI reads from repository state, idempotent by id.
  2. What is a safe at-most-once event? -> Haptic, analytics ping, scroll-to-top.
  3. Does SavedStateHandle help? -> It extends state-with-ack across process death for small pending flags.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: picks a tool. Senior: names the guarantee needed per event, enumerates failure windows, and moves critical outcomes to durable state.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "ticket booked" confirmation was a Channel event; users who backgrounded the app got no confirmation and booked twice.

questions.contextHtml: Release 5.12 migrated 40 screens from SingleLiveEvent to MutableSharedFlow<UiEvent>(replay = 1) to "fix events lost when the app is backgrounded". Crash rate is flat, but support reports spike: users see the "Added to cart" snackbar again after rotating the product page, and tablet users get a duplicated "Order placed" screen push (about 1.1% of tablet sessions). Play vitals show tablets rotate 3x more than phones. Logs show Navigating to confirmation twice with the same orderId within 200 ms of onConfigurationChanged.
questions.promptHtml: Why did the migration cause this, how do you stop the bleeding, and what do you ship long term?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Set replay back to 0." That reintroduces the original loss bug and ignores why the team set replay=1.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which screens use navigation events vs snackbars? How many collectors per flow? Is collection under repeatOnLifecycle? Any resetReplayCache() calls?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remote-config kill switch or a hotfix that handles navigation events with an id-based "already handled" guard in the screen; for snackbars, accept the repeat temporarily.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) replay=1 replays the last event to the new collector after rotation. (b) Two collectors (Activity plus Fragment) each receive broadcast copies. (c) Collection restarts on STARTED re-entry. (d) Red herring: tablet-specific layout; rotation count only exposes it.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log collector start/stop with subscription count (subscriptionCount on SharedFlow); reproduce with adb shell settings put system accelerometer_rotation toggling or AndroidStudio rotate; check Play vitals correlation by form factor.
  5. Root cause: replay stores the last emitted event, and every new subscriber, including the one created by rotation, receives it. The migration fixed loss by buying duplication.
  6. Fix: Short term: id-guard. Long term: apply the decision tree: navigation and persistent messages become state with ack (pendingNavigation: Route? consumed with onNavigated()); cosmetic effects stay on a Channel with onUndeliveredElement logging.
// state-with-ack for navigation
data class UiState(val navigateTo: Route? = null)
fun onNavigated() = _ui.update { it.copy(navigateTo = null) }
  1. Prevention: A test that rotates mid-flow (ActivityScenario.recreate()/StateRestorationTester) and asserts one navigation; a design review rule "no replay>0 on event flows".
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use resetReplayCache() after emit: it races with collectors that are about to subscribe and brings back loss.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did QA not catch it? -> Phones rotate rarely in tests; add rotation to the standard regression checklist.
  • Can you keep SharedFlow? -> For broadcast, non-critical events yes, but not for navigation.
  • What about replay=1 with an Event<T> wrapper (consumed flag)? -> Rebuilds SingleLiveEvent semantics, with the same multi-consumer flaw.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A migration PR was praised for deleting the "ugly" SingleLiveEvent class; the real cost showed up two releases later as duplicate pushes on foldables, where posture changes recreate the Activity repeatedly.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Reverts replay without a plan for the original bug.
  • Hire: Identifies replay duplication and moves navigation to state.
  • Strong hire: Adds per-event guarantee classification, rotation regression tests, and subscription-count diagnostics.

questions.promptHtml: How do you design snackbar and toast messages from the ViewModel so that none are lost, none are doubled, and queued messages show one after another?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the most common "event" in real apps; a good answer touches state, ids and Compose suspend semantics.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Keep a list of messages with unique ids in UiState. The UI shows the first one with showSnackbar (a suspend call that waits until dismissal), then tells the ViewModel the id was shown, which removes it. Ids prevent two identical strings collapsing and prevent a late ack from deleting a newer message.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• SnackbarHostState.showSnackbar suspends until the snackbar is dismissed or times out; concurrent calls are serialized by an internal mutex, so one at a time is built in. You still need your own queue because the ViewModel may produce messages while the UI is gone.
  • Toasts are not tied to composition; they can appear while the app is backgrounded (system toasts) and should usually be consumed only in foreground (guide's "when state needs to be consumed" principle).
  • Message identity: data class UserMessage(val id: Long, val text: String) with id from a counter or UUID; the ack uses the id.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
data class UserMessage(val id: Long, val text: String)
data class UiState(val messages: List<UserMessage> = emptyList())

class VM : ViewModel() {
    private val _ui = MutableStateFlow(UiState())
    val ui = _ui.asStateFlow()
    fun post(text: String) = _ui.update { it.copy(messages = it.messages + UserMessage(nextId++, text)) }
    fun shown(id: Long) = _ui.update { s -> s.copy(messages = s.messages.filterNot { it.id == id }) }
    private var nextId = 0L
}

@Composable
fun Messages(ui: UiState, host: SnackbarHostState, onShown: (Long) -> Unit) {
    ui.messages.firstOrNull()?.let { m ->
        LaunchedEffect(m.id) { host.showSnackbar(m.text); onShown(m.id) }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• A single String? field: second message overwrites the first.
  • Acking after showSnackbar returns, but also on cancellation (rotation) if you use finally; then you lose a message the user never saw.
  • Showing a toast from a Channel while the app is backgrounded.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Cancelled showSnackbar due to rotation: lost? -> Not if you only ack after normal return; the message stays in state and reshows.
  2. Should messages be saved across process death? -> Rarely; transient feedback.
  3. Cap on queue size? -> Yes; drop oldest after N or you stack stale messages.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: String? plus null-after-show. Senior: list with ids, ack by id, cancellation-safe ack, foreground-only consumption.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An error snackbar and a success snackbar landed within 100 ms; the single-field version showed only the success.

questions.promptHtml: Defend or attack the claim "events as state is always the right answer". Where does it get awkward?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Senior engineers should hold the official guidance critically; the strongest answers show both the principle and its costs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The principle is sound: state is replayable and testable, and a missed render is recoverable. The costs are real: every screen needs an ack function, state fields that are "pending commands" blur the model, at-least-once duplicates must be tolerated, and some effects (haptics, scroll-to-item, focus request) are commands, not facts. I use state for anything user-visible and consequential, and a small lifecycle-aware effect channel for cosmetic commands, with the trade-off documented.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Pro: survives rotation and recomposition, testable by asserting state, one source of truth, no Channel cancellation races, works with Compose previews.
  • Con 1: ack boilerplate and the risk of forgetting it (message re-shows forever).
  • Con 2: ack races and repeated identical messages (need ids).
  • Con 3: modeling pain: "scroll list to top after refresh" is a command; scrollToTop: Boolean flags in UiState are a smell that you ack to clear.
  • Con 4: mixing "pending commands" with "facts about the screen" in one data class weakens the idempotent-render property (UiState -> UI should be a pure function; a pending command is not a fact).
  • Alternative for commands: UiState holds scrollToken: Int and the UI scrolls when the token changes, no ack needed (idempotent per token via LaunchedEffect(token) plus rememberSaveable last-handled token).
  • Bridge: an effect Channel only for non-critical, cancellable, at-most-once UI commands.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// token instead of ack for a pure UI command
data class ListUiState(val items: List<Item>, val scrollToTopToken: Int = 0)

@Composable
fun List(ui: ListUiState, listState: LazyListState) {
    var handled by rememberSaveable { mutableIntStateOf(ui.scrollToTopToken) }
    LaunchedEffect(ui.scrollToTopToken) {
        if (ui.scrollToTopToken != handled) { listState.animateScrollToItem(0); handled = ui.scrollToTopToken }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Dogma: forcing "isFocusRequested" booleans into the ViewModel.
  • Ack functions that are public API of the ViewModel, tempting other callers to call them.
  • Using events-as-state for non-idempotent commands (charge, delete).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. A rule to decide? -> Does losing it harm the user, and is replay harmless? Harm -> state; harmless cosmetic -> effect.
  2. Token vs ack? -> Token keeps the ViewModel unaware of the UI's consumption; ack is simpler but chattier.
  3. How would you document the choice? -> A short ADR in the repo listing which events use which mechanism.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: parrots the guide or the opposing blog. Senior: gives the criteria, shows the cost, offers token and effect-channel escapes, and writes the rule down for the team.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A codebase with 60 xxxShown() functions showed ack-forgetting bugs in code review; a shared message queue helper removed most of them.

questions.contextHtml: A fintech app (1.2M DAU) has "Confirm transfer": the ViewModel calls the transfer API (p95 6 s) and then sends NavigateToReceipt(txId) through Channel<Effect>(RENDEZVOUS) collected in repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED). Support reports about 0.4% of transfers: money moved, but user stays on the "Processing..." spinner after switching to a banking-OTP app and back, and then taps Confirm again. Duplicate-transfer rate rose 0.1% (guarded server-side by an idempotency key, 70% of the time). No crashes; logs show transfer ok txId=... followed by nothing on the client.
questions.promptHtml: What happened, and how do you redesign the flow?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use Channel.UNLIMITED." Still volatile on process death and still invisible, and it does not address re-submission.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the client process get killed while the OTP app is foreground? Is the send suspended when the UI is stopped? Is the transfer idempotent end to end? Does the Confirm button disable while in flight?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable Confirm while inFlight, show transaction state from repository on resume, and re-check server transaction status by idempotency key when the screen returns.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The event was sent while STOPPED; the collector was cancelled, and with RENDEZVOUS the send suspended until the collector reappeared, or was cancelled with the viewModelScope after process death. (b) Process death while in the OTP app lost both ViewModel and event. (c) UI cancelled mid-receive. (d) Red herring: network flakiness; the transfer succeeded.
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce with "Don't keep activities" and adb shell am kill <pkg> while in OTP app; add onUndeliveredElement logging; check process-start-reason from ApplicationExitInfo.
  5. Root cause: The outcome of a consequential command was modeled as an ephemeral event with at-most-once delivery, tied to a consumer lifecycle shorter than the producer's work.
  6. Fix: Persist the transfer (id, status) in the repository/DB; ViewModel exposes TransferUiState derived from it (Pending, Succeeded(txId)); UI navigates on Succeeded with a back-stack-safe guard and an ack; on process restore, the screen re-reads status by idempotency key.
sealed interface TransferUi { object Idle: TransferUi; object Pending: TransferUi; data class Done(val txId: String): TransferUi }
  1. Prevention: A chaos test "kill process mid-transfer"; rule "consequential outcomes = durable state"; alert on client log gap transfer ok without receipt shown.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not make the ViewModel use GlobalScope to survive; durability belongs to a repository/WorkManager job (A5), not a longer-lived coroutine.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the user force-stops? -> Server status by idempotency key on next launch decides the first screen.
  • Do you still need the ack? -> Yes, to avoid re-navigating when the user comes back to Confirm.
  • Could WorkManager own the transfer? -> Yes for reliability; surface the result as a Flow of status.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An incident review traced "missing confirmation" tickets to a three-line effect channel written for a demo; the fix was renaming the concept from "event" to "transfer status".

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Increases the buffer size.
  • Hire: Moves the result to state and disables duplicate submission.
  • Strong hire: Persists the command outcome, uses idempotency keys, tests process death, and names the delivery guarantee.

questions.promptHtml: In MVI libraries such as Orbit, a "side effect" flow sits beside state. What delivery semantics does it have, and when is it the right tool?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Teams adopting MVI inherit a side-effect stream. The signal is whether you know it is the same Channel trade-off with nicer packaging.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: MVI containers expose state (a StateFlow) and a one-shot side-effect stream. Orbit's postSideEffect is called inside intent { } alongside reduce. Under the hood it is a buffered, single-consumer stream, so it carries the Channel properties: queued while nobody collects (verify exact caching/replay behavior in the Orbit version you use), single consumer, lost on process death, and cancellable in flight. It is right for cosmetic commands; it is the wrong place for outcomes users depend on.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Reducer purity: reduce is a pure state transition; side effects are explicitly separated so state stays replayable and testable.
  • Orbit's test utilities let you assert emitted states and side effects separately, which is the main ergonomic win over hand-rolled Channels.
  • Danger: teams route everything through postSideEffect (navigate, errors) because it is convenient, recreating the guidance-violating pattern. The library does not stop you.
  • Collecting in Compose follows the same rules as Q052: collect inside an effect with lifecycle awareness and hold the SnackbarHostState in the UI.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Orbit-style (API shape; verify against your Orbit version)
sealed interface CartEffect { data class Toast(val text: String) : CartEffect }

class CartViewModel : ViewModel(), ContainerHost<CartState, CartEffect> {
    override val container = container<CartState, CartEffect>(CartState())
    fun add(id: String) = intent {
        reduce { state.copy(adding = true) }
        postSideEffect(CartEffect.Toast("Added"))
        reduce { state.copy(adding = false) }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling postSideEffect for navigation after a payment.
  • Collecting the side-effect flow in two places.
  • Testing only state and ignoring the effect stream.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do you draw the line between effect and state? -> Consequence and replay-safety (Q060).
  2. Does Orbit make effects exactly-once? -> No library can across process death.
  3. Would you hand-roll instead? -> For a small app a Channel plus a documented rule is enough; a library earns its place with testing tools and team convention.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "side effects are one-time events". Senior: knows it is a Channel in a framework, assigns it only cosmetic work, and keeps consequential outcomes in state.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team used postSideEffect(NavigateHome) after sign-out; users backgrounding mid-request stayed on a signed-out screen.

questions.promptHtml: How do you unit test ViewModel events for each approach (state-with-ack, Channel effects, SharedFlow)? What do you assert, and what traps exist?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Testability is a main reason to choose an approach; interviewers check you can actually write these tests.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: For state-with-ack I assert plain state transitions: trigger, assert userMessage set, call userMessageShown(), assert null. No coroutines gymnastics beyond runTest. For Channel/SharedFlow effects I collect with Turbine (test { awaitItem() }) started before triggering the action; with SharedFlow replay 0 collecting after the trigger misses the event. State tests are simpler, which is itself an argument for the state approach.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Use runTest with an injected StandardTestDispatcher/UnconfinedTestDispatcher as Dispatchers.Main (see the dispatcher-injection discussion in the testing chunk).
  • Turbine is a third-party library (app.cash.turbine); flow.test { ... } collects in a background coroutine and awaitItem() suspends with a timeout. Always end with cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents() or ensureAllEventsConsumed().
  • For SharedFlow, collect first with UnconfinedTestDispatcher so the subscription exists before emit.
  • Do not test lifecycle loss in ViewModel tests; test it in a UI/instrumented test with ActivityScenario.recreate() or Compose StateRestorationTester.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Test fun refresh_offline_showsMessageThenAck() = runTest {
    val vm = NewsViewModel(FakeRepo(offline = true))
    vm.refresh(); advanceUntilIdle()
    assertEquals("No internet", vm.ui.value.userMessage)
    vm.userMessageShown()
    assertNull(vm.ui.value.userMessage)
}

@Test fun pay_emitsSnackbar() = runTest {
    val vm = PayViewModel(FakePay())
    vm.effects.test {                 // collect first
        vm.onPay()
        assertEquals(Effect.Snack("Paid"), awaitItem())
        cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents()
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling the action then vm.effects.first(): on SharedFlow(replay=0) it hangs or misses.
  • Forgetting to set Dispatchers.Main, causing viewModelScope failures.
  • Asserting state equality after an event with StateFlow conflation and missing an intermediate state.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you test the double-navigation bug? -> A UI test that recreates the Activity and asserts back-stack size.
  2. Why no delay() in tests? -> runTest uses virtual time; advanceUntilIdle.
  3. How do you test ack races? -> Post two messages, ack the first id, assert second remains.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use Turbine". Senior: explains collect-before-trigger, splits unit vs UI tests, and notes state tests as an argument for the pattern.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A flaky test suite came from effect tests collecting after the trigger; they passed locally on UnconfinedTestDispatcher and failed on CI under a different scheduling order.

questions.contextHtml: A 9-year-old app (3M MAU, 140 screens, mixed Java/Kotlin, LiveData everywhere) has an Event<T>/SingleLiveEvent helper used in about 220 places. The team is adopting Compose screen by screen. Constraints: weekly releases, no big-bang, Crashlytics baseline crash-free sessions 99.6%, and the last "events" rewrite caused a duplicate-order incident. About 60% of usages are snackbars/toasts, 25% navigation, 10% dialogs/permissions, 5% miscellaneous (haptics, analytics).
questions.promptHtml: How do you migrate without regressions and without a rewrite freeze?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Replace all with SharedFlow in one PR." No classification, no staged rollout, no tests.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which usages are consequential? Are there multi-observer cases? Do any Java callers depend on the API? What test coverage exists on these screens? Can we flag per screen?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Freeze new usages of SingleLiveEvent via a lint rule/detekt baseline; nothing else changes yet.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (risks): (a) Multi-observer usages silently change behavior. (b) Navigation moved to wrong lifetime and double-fires. (c) Dialogs/permission requests lost in background. (d) Red herring: raw perf; effects are cheap.
  4. How I'd verify each: Inventory by script/grep and classify into snackbar/navigation/dialog/misc; for each class write a characterization test (rotation, background-foreground, double tap) on the existing implementation before touching it.
  5. Root cause: The risk is not the API; it is that each usage encodes an implicit delivery contract nobody wrote down.
  6. Fix (plan): Per class: snackbars -> list-with-ids state (Q059); navigation -> state-with-ack or UI-owned lambda (Q054); dialogs -> dialog: DialogState? in UiState; permissions -> UI-owned rememberLauncherForActivityResult; misc -> lifecycle-aware effect Channel. Migrate screen-by-screen alongside the Compose move, behind the existing LiveData facade (asLiveData() adapter) so Java screens keep compiling. Staged rollout 1% -> 10% -> 100% by percentage release, watching crash-free sessions and duplicate-order metric.
  7. Prevention: ADR with the decision table; lint/detekt rule banning SingleLiveEvent and MutableSharedFlow(replay = >0) for events; screen tests including recreate().
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not introduce a generic Event wrapper over StateFlow; it hides the guarantee. I would not migrate low-traffic dead screens; deletion beats migration.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A Java Fragment still observes? -> Keep a LiveData adapter until the screen moves.
  • Release goes bad on one screen? -> Revert that screen's migration commit; each is independent.
  • How measure success? -> Events-related bug tickets and duplicate-action analytics trending down.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The inventory showed 31 of 220 usages were dead code; deleting them first cut the effort 14% and cleared a "mystery" duplicate-navigation path.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Global replace with one mechanism.
  • Hire: Classifies usages and migrates incrementally with tests.
  • Strong hire: Characterization tests, staged rollout with metrics, lint ban, adapters for Java, and deletion of dead usages first.

questions.contextHtml:
A tablet master-detail app uses an Activity-scoped shared ViewModel between ListFragment and DetailFragment (both visible on tablets, one at a time on phones). Bug reports: on tablets, tapping Delete shows "Item deleted" snackbar sometimes in the list pane and sometimes not at all, and navigation to the list "pops twice" on 1.8% of delete actions. Phones are fine.

class ItemsViewModel(private val repo: ItemsRepo) : ViewModel() {
    private val _events = Channel<ItemEvent>(Channel.BUFFERED)
    val events = _events.receiveAsFlow()
    fun delete(id: String) = viewModelScope.launch {
        repo.delete(id)
        _events.send(ItemEvent.Deleted(id))
    }
}
// ListFragment and DetailFragment both do:
viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
    viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
        vm.events.collect { if (it is ItemEvent.Deleted) handle(it) }
    }
}

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use SharedFlow so both receive it." Both then handle navigation, so duplicate popping becomes guaranteed.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which fragment should show the snackbar and which should navigate? Does the layout change on rotation? Is the VM scoped to the Activity?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Make only one fragment (the host) collect events, or add id-based dedupe per event, as a hotfix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Channel receiveAsFlow is fan-out: with two collectors each event goes to one of them, so snackbar location is effectively random. (b) The delete event also triggers pop in whichever collector wins, and rotation re-collects, causing a second pop. (c) Fragment view recreation in the tablet back stack leaves a stale collector. (d) Red herring: repository delete threading.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log collector identity in collect; observe alternating handling; check FragmentManager for lingering collectors.
  5. Root cause: Two concurrent consumers on a single-consumer stream; "delivered exactly once" with several consumers is the case the official guide warns about.
  6. Fix: Push the concern upward as the guide advises: one owner (the Activity/host or a parent composable) consumes deletion feedback; or model it as state: ItemsUiState(deletedMessage: Message?, selected: Item?) where the list pane renders the snackbar and the detail pane renders from selected == null. Layout decides what the state means on tablet vs phone.
data class ItemsUi(val items: List<Item>, val selectedId: String?, val message: UserMessage?)
fun delete(id: String) = viewModelScope.launch {
    repo.delete(id)
    _ui.update { it.copy(selectedId = null, message = UserMessage(nextId++, "Item deleted")) }
}
  1. Prevention: Rule: an event stream has a documented single owner; a test with both fragments started that asserts one snackbar.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not broadcast with SharedFlow and rely on each fragment to filter; consumption responsibility becomes implicit.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if both panes legitimately need to react? -> State: both render from it; neither consumes an event.
  • Why does phone behave? -> Only one fragment is started at a time, so there is one collector.
  • Compose version? -> Same: hoist consumption to the parent composable.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A foldable launch exposed it: the second screen made two collectors visible simultaneously, and "random" snackbars were the first symptom.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Switches to SharedFlow.
  • Hire: Identifies fan-out and restricts to one consumer.
  • Strong hire: Moves to state so layout decides meaning, and adds a two-pane test.

questions.contextHtml: You are the tech lead of a 12-engineer team building a ride-hailing app (800k DAU). Engineers argue in PR reviews: half insist on Channel for "one-time" effects, half cite the official guide and want everything as state. The current backlog of event bugs: 14 "snackbar after rotation", 6 "double navigation", 3 "payment screen lost", over a quarter. New hires get conflicting advice. You have one sprint to settle it.
questions.promptHtml: What do you decide, how do you roll it out, and how do you keep it from becoming dogma?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Picks a side by taste ("Channels are simpler") without data or per-event criteria.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which events caused customer harm vs cosmetic noise? What is our test coverage? How many screens are Compose vs Views? Who owns shared UI infrastructure?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fix the three "payment screen lost" cases first by moving them to durable state; they are the only harmful ones.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (why the bug rate persists): (a) No shared contract per event type. (b) Mixed mechanisms in one screen. (c) No tests for rotation/background. (d) Red herring: the choice of library.
  4. How I'd verify each: Triage the 23 bugs by event type and mechanism; check which mechanism each used; reproduce a sample with rotation and background tests.
  5. Root cause: Disagreement about a tool, when the real variable is the required delivery guarantee per event.
  6. Fix: A one-page ADR with a decision table: consequential/visible-state-changing -> UiState with ack (ids); persistent messages -> message queue with ids; pure UI commands (scroll, focus) -> token in state; non-critical cosmetic (haptics, analytics) -> single-owner Channel with onUndeliveredElement logging. Provide shared helpers (message queue, effect collector) so the right path is the easy path. Add detekt rules (no SingleLiveEvent, no replay>0 event flows) and screen test templates with recreate().
  7. Prevention: Review checklist item "what happens on rotation, background and process death?"; track event-bug count each quarter; revisit the ADR when the official guidance changes (verify current wording on the UI events page).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not ban Channels outright, and I would not mandate state-everything; both ignore that cost and guarantee vary per event. I would not rewrite working screens; apply the rule on touch.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A senior refuses state for focus requests? -> Accept token-in-state or the effect channel; the ADR allows it with a reason.
  • How do you measure? -> Bug tickets tagged "event", duplicate-action analytics, crash-free sessions.
  • KMP shared ViewModels? -> State-based events travel better across platforms than Channels, favouring state for shared code.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The argument ended once the team put the 23 bugs on a table by event type; 100% of the harmful ones used a Channel for a consequential outcome, while the cosmetic ones were harmless either way.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Chooses by preference.
  • Hire: Cites the guide and states a rule with exceptions.
  • Strong hire: Data-driven triage, per-event guarantee table, shared helpers, lint/test enforcement, and a review cadence.
